701.title: Holy ground again (Joshua 5:13–15)
701.hook: a captain of the Lord's host tells Joshua to loose his shoe, as Moses once did
701.howItsDone: In synagogue, kohanim take off their shoes before they go up to recite the priestly blessing over the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve stones from the riverbed, set up so children would ask. Your line was what mean these stones. Did anyone ask about yours? Today, near Jericho, a stranger with a sword. Day seven hundred one.

"Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?" That's Joshua's question, and it's a fair one. He's near Jericho, the walled city his people have to face. He looks up, and a man is standing in front of him with a drawn sword in his hand. Joshua doesn't run. He walks straight up to him and asks the first thing a general would want to know. Whose side are you on? The answer he gets is one he didn't ask for, and it changes the question.
screen: `NEAR JERICHO.` → `A MAN WITH A DRAWN SWORD.` → `WHOSE SIDE ARE YOU ON?`

segments.voice: The stranger's first word, in Hebrew, is lo. No. Not for you, not for your enemies. I have come as captain of the host of the Lord. Joshua falls on his face and asks what his lord wants of his servant. And the reply isn't a battle plan. It's this: take your shoe off your foot, for "the place whereon thou standest is holy." If you've been with us through the Torah, you've heard that sentence before. Moses at the burning bush, the first time God speaks to him: put off thy shoes, "for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Now Moses is gone, and his assistant, at the start of his own hardest days, hears the same words. The way Moses began, Joshua begins. Look closely and there's a small difference. Moses is told to take off his shoes. Joshua is told to take off his shoe, just one. The text doesn't say why. Then notice what the text does next. Nothing. The captain doesn't deliver a message. The scene ends: and Joshua did so. So what was the visit for? One answer in the Talmud says the captain came because the people had let their Torah study slip in the camp. Another way to read it is just as it stands: the message was the ground. Before the walls, before strategy, before anyone asks whose side God is on, Joshua is asked to stand still, barefoot, and know where he is.
screen: `LO: NO.` · `TAKE OFF YOUR SHOE.` · `AS MOSES DID AT THE BUSH.` · then, large: `AND JOSHUA DID SO.` · then: `THE MESSAGE WAS THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still for a minute, barefoot. If you can, take off your shoes, or one shoe, and stand. If standing isn't possible, sit and put your bare feet flat on the floor. Feel what's under you: wood, tile, carpet, cold or warm. This is an ordinary floor, in an ordinary room. Stand on it as if it mattered. No need to ask anything, or to work anything out. If you pray, this can be your prayer: just standing here. Let the rest of the time be still. The bell holds the time.
Holy ground again. The words Moses heard at the bush, heard by Joshua near Jericho, with one shoe off and no sides taken. Today's word.
Your line: holy ground again. Today, at one ordinary spot, a doorway, a kitchen, a parking lot, stop for one breath and notice where you're standing. Day seven hundred one.

702.title: The walls of Jericho (Joshua 6)
702.hook: six days of silent circling, then shofar blasts and a shout
702.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah the shofar is sounded in synagogue in a set series of calls, among them teruah, a run of quick short blasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger with a sword, and Joshua barefoot. Your line was holy ground again. Did you stop for a breath somewhere ordinary? Today, the city itself. Day seven hundred two.

For six days, the only sound around Jericho is the shofar. Armed men walk in front. Then seven priests, blowing seven rams' horns as they go. Then the ark. Then everyone else. Row after row of feet, and not one human voice. The instruction was clear: no shouting, no talking, not a word from your mouth until the day you're told. Once around the walls, back to the camp for the night. The next morning, again. Behind its walls, Jericho is shut tight, facing an army that doesn't attack.
screen: `SIX DAYS OF SHOFAR.` → `NOT ONE HUMAN VOICE.` → `AN ARMY THAT DOESN'T ATTACK.`

segments.voice: On the seventh day they rise at dawn and go around, not once, but seven times. On the seventh circuit the priests blow, and Joshua finally gives the word: shout, for the Lord has given you the city. The people raise a great shout, and "the wall fell down flat." Notice what the story leaves out. No battering ram. No ladders. No tunnel under the wall. The city is taken by a strange discipline: patience, silence, repetition, and then one sound at the right moment. The instruction had said it plainly: no word from your mouth until the day I bid you shout, "then shall ye shout." Now listen to the shout itself. The Hebrew for that great shout is teruah. It's also the name of a shofar call. When the Torah describes Rosh Hashanah, it calls it a day of teruah, a day of blowing the horn. So the same word holds a people's cry and the ram's horn of the new year. Some readers hear in Jericho a picture of the Days of Awe: circle, wait, keep quiet, and then let out the sound you've been holding. And there's a hard part, and the book doesn't hide it. The city is put under the ban, and its people are killed, and readers wrestle with that command. Inside the destruction, one promise holds. Before the city burns, the two spies go into Rahab's house and bring out her and her whole family, as they swore they would. The spies kept their word.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `NO RAM, NO LADDER: SILENCE.` · `TERUAH: A SHOUT, A SHOFAR CALL.` · then, large: `THE WALL FELL DOWN FLAT.` · then: `RAHAB'S FAMILY BROUGHT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk around something in silence. A table, a chair, a bed, the room you're in. Walk slowly, once around, without a word. Then again. Notice your feet, the edges, what you usually walk past without seeing. If you can't walk, let your eyes go slowly around the edges of the room instead, once, then again. Keep the silence the whole way. When you stop, stand or sit still and let the quiet settle before anything else is said. The bell holds the time.
Teruah. A great shout, and also a shofar call: the sound that brought down the walls of Jericho after six silent days of circling.
Your line: circle, then shout. Today, be patient and quiet with one thing that won't move yet, and when the moment comes, say what needs saying. Day seven hundred two.

703.title: Achan (Joshua 7)
703.hook: one man's hidden theft brings trouble on everyone
703.howItsDone: Jewish confession on Yom Kippur is said in the plural, "we have sinned", by the whole congregation together, and the Talmud's reading of Achan's story is cited for the idea that a Jew who sins remains a Jew.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teruah, the walls of Jericho, silence and then the shout. Your line was circle, then shout. Did you wait for the right moment to speak? Today, what someone carried out of Jericho. Day seven hundred three.

The book tells us the secret before anyone in the story knows it. Chapter seven opens: the children of Israel broke faith, because a man named Achan took things from Jericho that were forbidden, and hid them. Joshua has no idea. He sends a small force up to Ai, a little town, an easy win after Jericho. They run. Men die on the slope. And the hearts of the people melt like water, the same words Rahab used about Jericho's fear. Joshua tears his clothes and lies on his face before the ark until evening.
screen: `THE READER KNOWS FIRST.` → `DEFEAT AT AI.` → `JOSHUA ON HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: God's answer to Joshua is short: "Israel hath sinned." Not Achan. Israel. One man took, one man hid, and the text names the whole people. That's the first thing this chapter teaches, and it's uncomfortable on purpose. In this story nobody is purely private. What one person buries reaches everyone. Then comes the search, and it's slow. In the morning the tribes come forward, and one tribe is taken by lot. Then that tribe's families, and one family is taken. Then its households. Then its men, one by one. The circle narrows, step by step, and all through it, Achan says nothing. Only when the lot falls on him by name does Joshua speak to him, and he speaks gently: my son, give glory to God, tell me what you've done, hide it not from me. And Achan tells it, step by step. I saw. I coveted. I took. And they're hidden in the ground, inside my tent. Saw, wanted, took, hid: a whole hidden thing in one sentence. The ending is hard, and the text doesn't soften it: Achan and his household are stoned in a valley that gets the name Achor, trouble. The rabbis read the chapter's first verdict closely. The Talmud takes Israel hath sinned and notices the word Israel: even when Israel sins, the Talmud says, it is still Israel. Achan's wrong is called the people's, and the people keep their name.
screen: `ISRAEL HATH SINNED.` · `THE CIRCLE NARROWS.` · `SAW, COVETED, TOOK, HID.` · then, large: `STILL ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one hidden thing to yourself. Not to anyone else. Just to you. Settle, and breathe. Let something come up that you've kept buried: a thing you took, a word you didn't say, a habit you'd rather no one saw. Don't argue with it, and don't fix it right now. Just name it, silently, in plain words, the way Achan finally did: I saw, I wanted, I took, I hid. Then breathe out, and let it be known, at least by you. The bell holds the time.
Achan. The man who hid what he took from Jericho, whose silence brought trouble on everyone, whose people are still called Israel. Today's word.
Your line: one hidden thing affects all. Today, notice one way a private choice of yours reaches someone else. Day seven hundred three.

704.title: The Gibeonites (Joshua 9)
704.hook: tricked into a treaty, Israel keeps its oath anyway
704.howItsDone: In Jewish law vows and oaths are binding; the Kol Nidrei service on the eve of Yom Kippur addresses vows, and some Jews say bli neder, "without a vow", when promising something, to avoid an unintended oath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Achan, and what he buried in his tent. Your line was one hidden thing affects all. Did you notice a private choice reaching someone else? Today, a trick, and a promise. Day seven hundred four.

Dry bread, gone moldy and crumbling. Wineskins split and tied back together. Sandals patched and worn through. Clothes worn old. A group of strangers walks into Israel's camp at Gilgal carrying all of it like evidence. We've come from a very far country, they say. Look at our bread: it was warm from the oven the day we left. Make a treaty with us. They are lying. They live just over the hills, in Gibeon, and they've heard what happened at Jericho and Ai. The costume is the whole plan.
screen: `MOLDY BREAD, WORN SANDALS.` → `A VERY FAR COUNTRY.` → `THE COSTUME IS THE PLAN.`

segments.voice: And it works. The men of Israel look at the bread, taste it, and take it as proof. The text stops to point out what they skip: they didn't ask counsel of the Lord. Joshua makes peace with them, and the leaders of the congregation swear an oath to let them live. A few days later the truth comes out. The far country is next door. The people are furious, and they grumble against their leaders. And here the leaders say the sentence the chapter turns on: we have sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel, so we may not touch them. The oath was gotten by a lie. It still holds. The Gibeonites are spared, and they become, in the text's phrase, "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the people and for the altar. Did the oath bind because it was a valid contract? Some rabbis in the Talmud say no: it was made under false pretenses, but breaking it would have disgraced God's name in front of the nations. Either way, the promise outlives everyone in the room. Much later, the book of Samuel tells of a famine in King David's day, and traces it back to Saul, who had attacked the Gibeonites though Israel had sworn to them. The oath at Gilgal was still binding. A psalm describes the person who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and one line fits this chapter exactly: "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."
screen: `THEY DIDN'T ASK.` · `WE HAVE SWORN: WE MAY NOT TOUCH THEM.` · `GOD'S NAME, NOT A CONTRACT.` · `STILL BINDING IN DAVID'S DAY.` · then, large: `SWEARETH TO HIS OWN HURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a promise even when it costs. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one promise you made that has become inconvenient. Maybe it was made too fast. Maybe the situation changed. Maybe, like Israel's leaders, you'd have said no if you'd known more. Don't decide yet whether you're bound. Just picture keeping it: the actual hour it takes, the actual phone call. Notice what it costs, and what it would say about your word. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's line: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. The bell holds the time.
The Gibeonites. The neighbors who tricked Israel into a treaty, and were protected by the oath anyway. Today's word.
Your line: an oath is kept. Today, keep one small promise you'd rather slide out of, and keep it without announcing what it cost. Day seven hundred four.

705.title: Sun, stand still (Joshua 10:12–14)
705.hook: Joshua asks the sun to stand still at Gibeon
705.howItsDone: Jewish commentators read Joshua 10:12–14 in different ways, from a miracle in the heavens to a battle that ended before nightfall, and the passage is studied as part of the Former Prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gibeonites, and a treaty won by a trick. Your line was an oath is kept. Did you keep one promise you'd rather have dropped? Today, that oath gets tested. Day seven hundred five.

A messenger runs into the camp at Gilgal. Gibeon is surrounded. The kings of the region have joined forces against the city, because it made peace with Israel. Gibeon's message is short: don't abandon your servants; come quickly and save us. These are the same people who walked in with moldy bread and a lie. Joshua could let the treaty quietly fail. Instead he marches his army through the whole night, uphill, and falls on the attackers suddenly. And in the middle of that long day, he says something to the sky.
screen: `GIBEON SURROUNDED.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO TRICKED THEM.` → `A NIGHT MARCH TO SAVE THEM.`

segments.voice: Here are his words: "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon," and you, moon, in the valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood, and the moon stayed, until the people had won the day. Notice the shape of it. It's poetry, two lines that echo each other, sun and moon, Gibeon and Aijalon. And the text tells us where it comes from: it's written in the book of Jashar, a book the Bible names but doesn't include. So we're hearing an old song, quoted in the middle of the story. Now one word. The Hebrew for stand still is dom. In the Psalms the same word means be still, be silent. A reader can hear Joshua telling the sun, hush. Wait. Not yet. What happened in the sky? Jewish readers differ, and the tradition keeps both. Some take it as it sounds, a wonder in the heavens. Some medieval commentators, Gersonides among them, read it another way: the light held long enough, the battle ended before the sun went down, and that was the wonder. Then read the next verse. When the text marvels at this day, it doesn't marvel at the sun. It says there was no day like it, before or after, "that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man." The surprise isn't astronomy. It's that a person spoke, in the middle of keeping a hard promise, and God listened.
screen: `AN OLD SONG, SUN AND MOON.` · `THE BOOK OF JASHAR.` · `DOM: BE STILL, HUSH.` · `READERS DIFFER ON THE SKY.` · then, large: `GOD LISTENED TO A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one unhurried moment. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Settle, and let your breathing slow on its own. For the next two minutes there's nowhere to get to. Look at the light in the room, or outside: where it falls, how bright it is. Let the day stand still around you for a little while. Nothing to finish. Nothing to win. If a thought pulls you toward the next thing, tell it, quietly, the way Joshua spoke to the sun: hush, not yet. The bell holds the time.
Sun. The sun Joshua told to stand still over Gibeon, in an old song from the book of Jashar, on a day God listened to a person. Today's word.
Your line: hush, not yet. Today, in the busiest part of your day, stop the clock for ten slow breaths. Day seven hundred five.

706.title: Everyone gets a place (Joshua 13–19)
706.hook: long lists of borders give every tribe its portion
706.howItsDone: Jews read the border lists of Joshua 13–19 as part of studying the Former Prophets, and the daughters of Zelophehad, whose claim is told in Numbers and completed in Joshua, are studied as a model of asking for justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun over Gibeon, told to stand still. Your line was hush, not yet. Did you stop the clock for a few breaths? Today, the chapters it's easy to skim, and why they matter. Day seven hundred six.

The border goes up by a valley. It passes along to a spring of water. It turns toward a mountain, bends around, goes down to the sea. Then a list of towns, name after name after name, with their villages. Then the next tribe, and the next. For several chapters the book of Joshua reads like a surveyor's notebook. It's tempting to skip ahead to the next story. But every one of those names was somebody's front door, somebody's well, somebody's field. These chapters are where the wandering ends, and people get an address.
screen: `THE BORDER GOES UP, TURNS, GOES DOWN.` → `NAME AFTER NAME.` → `SOMEBODY'S FRONT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The text says the portions are given by lot. Nobody gets to grab the best valley; the land is shared out tribe by tribe, family by family. And each portion is named. Inside the lists there are moments. Five sisters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad, come before Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Their father had no sons. The Lord commanded Moses, they say, to give us a portion among our brothers. And they receive it, written into the borders with everyone else. A family that could have been left off the map is on it. Then the tribes of Joseph complain that their share is too small and the hill country too crowded. Joshua's answer: there's forest up there; go clear it, and it's yours. Room can be made. And one tribe gets no territory at all. Levi, the tribe of the priests and Levites, receives towns to live in among the others, but no portion of land, because, the text says, the Lord, the God of Israel, is their inheritance. Their place is a calling. A psalm uses the language of these chapters: lines, lots, portions. It sounds like someone looking at their own small share of the world and finding it enough: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage." The Hebrew for lines is chavalim, and it's the word the book of Joshua uses when shares of land fall to the tribe of Manasseh, in the same chapter as the five sisters. Everyone gets a place, and a place can be a field, a hillside you clear yourself, or a calling.
screen: `GIVEN BY LOT, NAMED BY NAME.` · `ZELOPHEHAD'S DAUGHTERS ON THE MAP.` · `CLEAR THE FOREST: ROOM IS MADE.` · `LEVI: GOD IS THEIR PORTION.` · then, large: `THE LINES ARE FALLEN IN PLEASANT PLACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: appreciate the place you have. Settle, and look around. This room, this chair, this street, this small piece of the world that is, for now, yours. It may not be the place you'd choose. Notice three things about it anyway: one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, one thing it gives you. Then think of the people who share your lines with you, at home, at work, next door. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words: the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places. The bell holds the time.
Everyone gets a place. The border lists of Joshua, where every tribe is given its portion by lot, five daughters claim theirs, and Levi's portion is God. Today's word.
Your line: everyone gets a place. Today, make room for someone: a seat at the table, a turn to speak, a name on the list. Day seven hundred six.

707.title: Caleb at eighty-five (Joshua 14:6–15)
707.hook: the old scout says he's as strong as ever: "give me this mountain"
707.howItsDone: Jews read Caleb's request as part of Joshua, the opening book of the Prophets, and remember Caleb, with Joshua, as the scouts who did not lose heart in Numbers 13–14.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the border lists, where every tribe and five daughters got a portion. Your line was everyone gets a place. Did you make room for someone? Today, one old man asks for his. Day seven hundred seven.

Eighty-five years old, and he's asking for ground held by giants. The people of Judah have come to Joshua at Gilgal, where the land is being shared out. One old man steps forward with a story. Forty years old was I, he says, when Moses sent me to spy out this land. I brought back word as it was in my heart. The others made the people's hearts melt. I didn't. Then he names his age today. And then he makes a request, and it isn't for a quiet valley.
screen: `GILGAL: THE LAND IS SHARED OUT.` → `FORTY WHEN MOSES SENT ME.` → `EIGHTY-FIVE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Caleb's speech is mostly memory. Back in the wilderness, at Kadesh-barnea, Moses sent scouts into this land. The book of Numbers tells it: the others came back talking about walled cities and giants, the sons of Anak, and the camp lost its nerve. Caleb said, let us go up at once. Now, at Gilgal, he tells it in his own words, and one phrase keeps coming back: he wholly followed the Lord. He says it about himself. He quotes Moses saying it. And the narrator says it again at the end. Then the surprise. He says he's as strong today as the day Moses sent him, strong for war, for going out and for coming in. And he asks: "Now therefore give me this mountain." Not a settled valley. The hill country of Hebron, where the Anakim live, in cities great and fortified. The very people whose size frightened the scouts all those years ago. Caleb doesn't promise a victory. He says, maybe the Lord will be with me, and I'll drive them out. Notice the shape of it. The fear that froze a whole camp is the exact place he asks to go. He has carried that mountain in his mind for forty-five years. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. The chapter ends quietly: the land had rest from war. The text doesn't make Caleb young again. It lets him be eighty-five, with a long memory and a hard request. Some readers hear a promise finally collected, since Moses swore the land his feet walked on would be his. Others hear something simpler: an old man who still wants a mountain to climb.
